Created by the migration and deposition of windblown sand as it is stopped by the rising Stillwater Mountains bordering to the north, east and west, the most dominant feature of the dune system is Sand Mountain which is approximately 3.5 miles long, 1 mile wide and 600 feet in height, making it the largest single dune in the Great Basin. The recreation area also includes the Sand Springs Pony Express Station historical site (1860) and the Sand Springs Desert Study Area. In addition to OHV riding on the open dunes, there are 23 miles of riding available on the designated trail system that was established in 2008 to preserve the Kearny Buckwheat habitat and protect the Sand Mountain Blue Butterfly which is endemic only to the Sand Mountain area. Overview Encompassing 154,000 acres, including just over 100,000 acres of already congressionally designated Wilderness, Sand to Snow National Monument is an ecological and cultural treasure and one of the most biodiverse areas in southern California, supporting more than 240 species of birds and twelve threatened and endangered wildlife species. Home to the region's tallest alpine mountain that rises from the floor of the Sonoran Desert, the monument also will protect sacred, archaeological and cultural sites, including an estimated 1,700 Native American petroglyphs. Featuring thirty miles of the world-famous Pacific Crest National Scenic Trail, the area is a favorite for camping, hiking, hunting, horseback riding, photography, wildlife viewing, and even skiing. Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia. In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot. Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers. However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television. Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate. Usman Khawaja Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year. Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.

Providing a picturesque backdrop to local communities, visitors can enjoy magnificent palm oases, snow-capped mountains, a national scenic trail, and wilderness areas. Its extensive backcountry can be accessed via trails from both the Coachella Valley and the alpine village of Idyllwild. Jointly managed by the BLM and the U.S. Forest Service, the Monument’s boundary encompasses about 280,000 acres, including public lands within the BLM’s California Desert Conservation Area and the San Jacinto Ranger District of the San Bernardino National Forest. The Monument includes two Federal wilderness areas -- the Santa Rosa and the San Jacinto. The Monument was established by an Act of Congress on October 24, 2000, "in order to preserve the nationally significant biological, cultural, recreational, geological, educational, and scientific values found in the Santa Rosa and San Jacinto Mountains" (Public Law 106-351). pages.text: Santander, Spain: A 2027 Guide to Its Waterfront Art Museums | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD Beloved by Spaniards, Santander Is Becoming a Global Art Mecca The easygoing beachfront city is getting a host of new and reborn museums. A 2014 transformation by landscape architect Fernando Caruncho more than doubled the size of Pereda Gardens, in the historic heart of Santander. Luis Fonseca, Getty Images By Eddi Fiegel Published October 20, 2026 Santander, a port city in northwestern Spain, has long seduced Spaniards with its spectacular horseshoe bay surrounded by rolling green hills and the Cantabrian mountains in the distance. But now the city, the capital of the Cantabria region, is poised to become an international art destination. In September 2026, the new arts, culture, and technology center Faro Santander opened in a historic building redesigned by acclaimed British architect David Chipperfield with a permanent collection including works by such legendary figures as el Greco, Rubens, Velázquez, and Goya. ( See all 25 of the destinations that made our list of the best places to visit in 2027. ) Meanwhile, 2027 will bring the first outpost of Madrid’s renowned Reina Sofía museum. The impressive Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria also has a new home designed by the Barcelona-based architecture practice Mendoza Partida. Art lovers are sure to appreciate the city’s walkable city center—where ornate, neoclassical façades sit alongside Baroque churches and grand, porticoed squares—and the wide sandy beaches lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas.

Yet you may not realize that probably the most expensive thing you will ever buy in your lifetime is your…retirement. Perhaps you've never thought of "buying" your retirement. Yet that is exactly what you do when you put money into a retirement nest egg. You are paying today for the cost of your retirement tomorrow. The cost of those future years is getting more expensive for most Americans, for two reasons. pages.text: Scientists Invent a Digestible, Paper-Based Battery That Can Power Swallowed or Implanted Medical Devices Skip to main content Researchers tested the battery in an RFID tag that can be rolled up in a capsule and swallowed. It can then transmit information about the digestive tract to a reader outside the body. MIT News Ingestible sensors provide a helpful way to monitor a person’s health from the inside. But finding effective ways to power them has been a challenge. They typically use either standard batteries, which contain harmful chemicals, or external sources that provide energy wirelessly. Now, scientists have created digestible, paper-based batteries that can power medical devices inside the body and eventually get broken down. The technology, described in the journal Nature Chemical Engineering on September 21, has so far been tested only in pigs. Nanotyrannus was long thought to be the very prey it's shown attacking in the illustration above, a young Tyrannosaurus rex . New evidence suggests it was a different class of dinosaur. Anthony Hutchings By Nicholas St. Fleur Published October 30, 2025 One of paleontology’s most polarizing problems is a teenage Tyrannosaurus rex with an identity crisis, and two scientists say they’ve solved it. In 1942, researchers from the Cleveland Museum of Natural History found the skull of a small theropod in Montana’s Hell Creek Formation. pages.text: Scottish football could pave way for 3pm TV blackout to end - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Games currently cannot be shown live between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday By Dale Johnson Football issues correspondent Published 29 October 2026 The first tentative steps to end the 3pm television blackout have been taken by Scottish football as it seeks offers for the next broadcast cycle. The SPFL has said that it is "flexible about the number of games" that will form part of the new deal, which will kick in from the 2029-30 season. BBC Sport understands this includes the possibility that broadcasters could bid to show all matches live - including those shown on a Saturday afternoon. The SPFL has created a tender with the greatest flexibility on the basis that the broadcaster does not seek to impose Article 48 of the Uefa Statutes. Article 48 allows leagues to set specific times when matches are banned from being shown live on television. It can only be enforced when 50% of matches in a country's top two divisions are played at the same time. While other parts of Europe have experimented with a blackout, it is now only present in the UK between 2:45pm and 5:15pm on a Saturday. You might have heard something about it . Paleontologists certainly have been jawing about it for a while, particularly how the movie’s dinosaurs stack up against the actual animals emerging from the rock.* But all the arguments about enfluffled dinosaurs and bunny hands have missed a more fundamental issue – could scientists ever recover enough intact dinosaur goo to populate a real Jurassic World? When the first Jurassic Park premiered in 1993, finding non-avian dinosaur DNA seemed a certainty. Two days before the official release of the movie Raúl Cano and colleagues announced that they had sequenced the DNA of a 135-120 million year old, amber-encased weevil. pages.description: These reptiles have roamed the oceans for 100 million years. We've put them at risk, but with a little help, they're rebounding.
pages.text: Sea turtles are surviving—despite us | National Geographic By Craig Welch Photographs by Thomas Peschak 25 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. To see all that’s hopeful and appalling about the way we treat sea turtles , there’s no better place to start than the Burj Al Arab Jumeirah hotel. This shimmering tower of blue and white glass is shaped like the jib of a sailboat bound for shore. It rose two decades ago on an artificial island amid the steel forest of construction cranes that is Dubai, part of the United Arab Emirates. A royal suite, at 8,396 square feet, comes with a private cinema and 17 pillow options. A weekend stay can top $50,000. I have come here, though, to see its nonpaying guests. ( Saving Sea Turtles) Passing a fleet of white Rolls-Royces, I meet British expat marine biologist David Robinson. We take an elevator down to a parking garage and walk by Lamborghinis to our destination: a labyrinth of pipes and plastic pools, the intensive care unit of an elaborate marine turtle hospital. In one tub a green sea turtle struggles with internal organ damage. One floor up, sick, critically endangered hawksbills fill aquariums. Blood seeps from a dying leatherback harpooned by an indigenous hunter near Indonesia’s Kei Islands. Leatherbacks are the largest of the seven sea turtle species and one of the most imperiled. pages.text: SearchGov | USAGov Skip to main content SearchGov Learn about SearchGov, the government search engine used on thousands of federal websites. SearchGov makes it easier for people to find the information they need from federal websites. As the search engine used by thousands of federal websites, SearchGov supports more than 200 million searches a year. SearchGov shares its history with USA.gov , beginning when internet entrepreneur Eric Brewer donated a powerful search engine to the government. In 2000, USA.gov, at the time named FirstGov.gov, debuted. It featured a search box that allowed users to search across government websites. In 2010, SearchGov expanded to serve agencies throughout the U.S. government. Learn how SearchGov helps agencies connect with the people they serve. pages.description: More than a hundred years after the USCGC Tampa sank in the deadliest U.S. naval loss of the Great War, its discovery sheds light on eleven Black sailors who made Coast Guard history.

On 26 September 1918, while operating in the English Channel, the USCGC Tampa was torpedoed and sunk by the German Submarine UB-91. All 131 persons on board were lost – the largest loss of life on any U.S. combat vessel during World War I. U.S. Coast Guard Heritage Assets Collection & Archives By Anissa Durham Published October 21, 2026 Amefike Changamire-Woodland is considered the family historian. Since the early 2000s, he has researched the life and legacy of his great-uncle Francis LeRoy Wilkes. Known to the family as “Uncle Frank,” Wilkes was a 21-year-old seaman aboard the USCGC Ta m pa during World War I. Wilkes was one of 11 Black Coast Guardsmen working on the cutter when, on Sept. 26, 1918, it was torpedoed by a German submarine. All 131 American and British men on the ship lost their lives that fateful night — the deadliest U.S. naval loss of the Great War. Some 80 years later, the fallen sailors were posthumously awarded the Purple Heart, making Wilkes and the ten other Black men onboard the first servicemen of color in the history of the Coast Guard to receive the honor. pages.description: Thousands of years ago, Florida’s coastline extended as much as 100 miles out beyond its present edge. Artifacts from that early era are now hidden underwater from Texas to Florida—and they could help settle major debates about when humans arrived in America.

Artifacts from that early era are now hidden underwater from Texas to Florida—and they could help settle major debates about when humans arrived in America. Archaeologists are diving the coastline that stretches from Texas to Florida to find artifacts from tribes that once lived there thousands of years ago—like these arrowheads from McFadden Beach, just outside present-day Houston. NPS The first blooms of spring. The first frost. The first dusting of snow. The signs and timing of the seasons is a finely tuned natural process. The interplay of temperature and daylight activates these changes and the subsequent plant and animal responses. A slight shift in any of these may mean that vegetation will no longer grow in a certain location or appear at a different time of year. Without plants, animals who eat them may struggle to survive or may have to move elsewhere to find better food. The consequences may extend to the entire ecosystem, including humans. In both Skagway and Nome, everyone agreed that spring is arriving earlier and fall is starting later. This not only makes for a longer growing season for gardeners, but it affects the arrival and departure timing of migratory animals that people hunt and may shift the location of where the animals are found. pages.text: Second International Decade for People of African Descent | United Nations Skip to main content UNFPA/Yuntong Man Learn & Participate: Decade for People of African Descent The Second International Decade for People of African Descent is a global effort to advance human rights, equality and opportunity for people of African descent around the world. Guided by the theme "People of African Descent: Recognition, Justice and Development," it brings together governments, the United Nations, civil society and communities to build a more just and inclusive future. Programme of Activities A Decade Dedicated to People of African Descent Recognition Justice Development Around 200 million people identifying themselves as being of African descent live in the Americas. Many millions more live in other parts of the world, outside of the African continent. The Second International Decade for People of African Descent builds on the achievements of the first Decade while accelerating action to address persistent inequalities, systemic racism, and the lasting impacts of racialised chattel enslavement and colonialism. Explore the multimedia library Experts talk about the importance of a Second International Decade for People of African Descent for 2025-2034. Photos Photos of the latest events from around the world. Videos Educational videos , interviews and highlights from General Assembly events. Secondary National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) and Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) and Particulate Matter (PM) Secondary National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for Nitrogen Dioxide (NO2) and Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) and Particulate Matter (PM) Basic Information Federal Register Citations 89 FR 105692 89 FR 26620 77 FR 20218 76 FR 46084 Docket Numbers EPA-HQ-OAR-2014-0128 On this page: Rule Summary Rule History Additional Resources Rule Summary On December 10, 2024, the Environmental Protection Agency revised an air quality standard to better protect public welfare against adverse effects caused by criteria air pollutants – including ecological effects such as damage to aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. This action revises the secondary National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) for oxides of sulfur ( SO X ) and retains the existing secondary standards for oxides of nitrogen (N oxides) and particulate matter (PM), aligning standards with the best-available science and ensuring air pollution concentrations remain at historically low levels.
